A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeceptionDecoded benchmark, authors, and three intent-centric tasks. The main text, tables, figures, mathematical notation, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 14 VLMs, human validation, modality and prompting analyses, fine-tuning transfer results, and an image-generator comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds transfer evaluations on Fakeddit and FakeNewsNet, an image-editing experiment, and dataset and annotation-disagreement analyses.

M1.justification: New Section 5.3 extends the synthesis procedure to editing original images with Nano Banana using intent-derived editing instructions. This adds an image-conditioned manipulation variant; the main GPT-4o/FLUX pipeline, detection prompts, and fine-tuning objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Transfer evaluation expands from MMFakeBench to include Reddit-based Fakeddit and FakeNewsNet's political and entertainment news. Section 5.3 also introduces localized image editing as a distinct manipulation scenario. These substantially broaden evaluation coverage beyond the retained benchmark and fully generated images.

E2.justification: The original 14 evaluated VLMs and the LLaVA-v1.6-7B/Qwen2.5-VL-7B pre/post fine-tuning comparisons are retained. The new editing study uses five existing detectors, while the original six-model FLUX/GPT-image comparison remains intact in Table 7.

E3.justification: The added transfer tests each use 1,000 randomly sampled instances balanced between real and fake. The editing pilot uses 200 source items with 200 edits per severity and the existing consistency-oriented prompt. Table 6 now reports only macro-F1, dropping macro-accuracy; the original training budget and core evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds a robustness comparison testing whether edited images are harder to detect than generated images. Appendix B.3 analyzes intent-category coverage, and Appendix C.1 adds a substantial disagreement audit separating intent ambiguity, annotator oversight, and generation defects, with four illustrated cases. Earlier ablations and robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify one evaluation run at temperature zero and retain three-annotator majority voting and Fleiss' kappa reporting. No repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice changes. The new disagreement breakdown provides descriptive diagnostic results without changing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results: Table 6 reports Qwen2.5-VL-7B macro-F1 of 32.69/41.96 on Fakeddit and 44.87/68.59 on FakeNewsNet before/after fine-tuning. New Table 8 reports GPT-4o accuracies of 48.0/61.0 on subtle/significant edited images versus 66.0/84.0 on generated images. Tables 9–10 add intent-frequency and disagreement counts. Existing main results and MMFakeBench macro-F1 values remain unchanged, while its macro-accuracy entries are removed.

T1.justification: The news-triplet notation, desired-influence/execution-plan formulation, and task definitions are retained. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v4's discussion of combinatorial intent configurations adds explanation rather than new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: Both versions claim benchmark utility, VLM fragility, and benefits from fine-tuning. v4 strengthens the training claim by asserting that synthesized data teaches generalizable implication-level intent reasoning, making this capability explicit in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. v3 reports transfer utility without this explicit mechanism claim.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation: Section 4.3 proposes primacy and instruction-authority biases for retained hint results; Appendix C.1 discusses subjective intent boundaries and generation-related ambiguity; Appendix B.3 interprets category frequencies as reflecting real-world salience. It also attributes transfer gains to learned implication-level reasoning and discusses editing-specific risks. Appendix A's existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 supplies a concrete data/code repository address and a reproducibility statement, documents sampling for the added transfer datasets, and identifies the editing model with example instructions. Existing model versions, fine-tuning hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and restrictions on releasing generation prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations on newer misinformation research, image editing, primacy, sycophancy, and misinformation patterns, including Li et al. (2025), Wang et al. (2023), Sharma et al. (2024), and Hobbs (2020). These support localized extensions; the central positioning against reader-inferred intent benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, introduction ending, transfer discussion, and conclusion, alongside expanded example explanations. Related-work headings are simplified; ethics and LLM-usage statements move before references; acknowledgments and reproducibility text are added. The overall method/results sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the editing illustration in Figure 5, four annotated disagreement examples in Figures 10–13, and three tables covering editing, intent frequencies, and disagreement reasons. Table 6 is redesigned around three benchmark columns. Existing figures are retained, with some relocation, renumbering, and substantially expanded captions.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3's single transfer benchmark and aggregate validation results, v4 provides broader transfer evidence, a realistic editing test, and clearer disclosure of annotation ambiguity. These improve empirical support and transparency. However, the stronger claim that fine-tuning compels implication-level reasoning is not isolated by the reported comparisons, tempering the net quality gain.
